title: Grassroots Movements

cards.h: When citizens do democracy between elections
cards.b:
The first lesson in this unit was about institutions: panchayats and municipalities. This one is about citizens' movements: people organising on their own to protect land, forests, wages, information and dignity.

Why do these belong under grassroots democracy? Because they deepen it. They give voice to people the parties miss and push the state to make laws such as the Right to Information Act (2005) and MGNREGA (2005).

Scholars give them different labels: non-party political formations (Rajni Kothari), new social movements (Gail Omvedt) or movements of the political society (Partha Chatterjee). In exams you are asked to explain their nature, give examples and judge their impact.

For environmental and women's movements in detail, see the final unit of this paper; here the focus is on how movements widen democracy.

Old and new social movements

Old movements (labour, peasants) fought for class and economic gains and often worked through parties. New social movements (Touraine, Melucci) are about identity, culture, environment and quality of life, and rely on civil society.

Resource mobilisation and political opportunity

McCarthy and Zald stress organisation and funds; Sidney Tarrow stresses the political openings that allow protest to succeed.

Rajni Kothari, "The Non-Party Political Process" (1984)

Argued that as parties lost touch with the poor, voluntary groups and local movements began to fill the gap. He saw them as a new "non-party political formation".

Partha Chatterjee, The Politics of the Governed (2004)

Distinguishes civil society (the middle class, who use rights and law) from political society (the poor, who negotiate with the state through collective claims).

Gail Omvedt, Reinventing Revolution (1993)

Treats Dalit, women's, farmers' and environmental movements as India's new movements, aiming to redefine the idea of social change.

cards.h: From Gandhian roots to the JP movement
cards.b:
• Bhoodan (1951): Vinoba Bhave began it at Pochampalli (then Hyderabad State) after a landlord offered land to the landless. It grew into the Gramdan idea of village ownership. Success in numbers was modest; in moral terms it was large.
  • Sarvodaya and the Gandhian constructive work tradition.
  • Navnirman Andolan (Gujarat, December 1973 to 1974): students and middle class against corruption and price rise forced the state government to resign.
  • Bihar Movement and JP's "Total Revolution" (1974): Jayaprakash Narayan led students against corruption. The Allahabad High Court's verdict (June 1975) and the Emergency (25 June 1975) followed. The Janata Party victory in 1977 grew out of this.

These movements showed that street politics could unseat governments, and the Emergency showed how fragile civil liberties were. They fed into the human rights groups of the late 1970s (PUCL, PUDR).

• MKSS (Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan): formed in 1990 in Rajasthan by Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey and Shankar Singh. From the mid-1990s it held jan sunwai (public hearings) where villagers compared muster rolls with real work. It started the demand for information, which became the RTI Act, 2005.
  • Right to Food: the petition in PUCL v. Union of India (2001) led to orders on midday meals and the Public Distribution System; later the National Food Security Act (2013).
  • MGNREGA (2005) includes a statutory social audit; Andhra Pradesh pioneered an independent social audit unit.
  • Land acquisition: protests in Singur and Nandigram (2006-07) fed the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.

cards.h: Livelihood and organisation: SEWA, farmers and tribal groups
cards.b:
• SEWA (Self-Employed Women's Association, Ahmedabad, 1972, founded by Ela Bhatt): a union of women in the informal sector with its own bank, cooperative and training. A model of organising where labour law barely reaches.
  • Farmers' movements: the Shetkari Sanghatana (Sharad Joshi, Maharashtra) argued that price policy was biased against "Bharat" in favour of "India". The Bharatiya Kisan Union (Mahendra Singh Tikait, western Uttar Pradesh, 1980s) and the Samyukta Kisan Morcha (2020-21) are later forms.
  • Tribal movements: the Jharkhand movement led to the state in 2000; Niyamgiri (Dongria Kondh, 2013) showed the Gram Sabha's power; PESA and the Forest Rights Act (2006) are the legal fruit.
  • Dalit movements: Dalit Panthers (1972), BSP and recent campaigns on atrocities (Una 2016).
  • Anti-arrack movement (Andhra Pradesh, 1992): rural women forced a ban on liquor sales.

The People's Plan Campaign (1996), launched by the Left Democratic Front government with T.M. Thomas Isaac as a key architect, gave local bodies 35-40% of the state's plan funds. Ward and Gram Sabhas held development seminars, volunteers prepared local plans and task forces drew in experts.

The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP, 1962) supplied thousands of volunteers with science and literacy skills. It is often called a people's science movement.

Why it matters: it shows how movements and institutions can work together. Putnam's idea of social capital (Making Democracy Work, 1993) helps explain it, as Kerala has dense associational life and high literacy. Critics note that political party rivalry later weakened the experiment, and funds were not always maintained.

Other examples: participatory budgeting in Pune; Mohalla Sabhas in Delhi (2015); Kudumbashree (Kerala, 1998) for poverty alleviation through women's neighbourhood groups.

Movements have left behind practical tools that ordinary people can use:

  • Right to Information: an application to any public authority, with a 30-day reply time; first appeal; appeal to the Information Commission.
  • Social audit: villagers check records against reality, as in MGNREGA (Section 17 of the Act). Meghalaya was the first state to pass a Social Audit law (2017).
  • Jan sunwai: public hearing where officials answer questions in front of villagers.
  • Citizens' Charters: introduced in 1997 after a conference of Chief Ministers; critics say they lack legal force.
  • Gram Sabha: the legal forum under Article 243A that can approve beneficiary lists and plans.
  • Public interest litigation: relaxed standing since the late 1970s (Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer). Upendra Baxi called this "social action litigation".
  • Lokpal and Lokayuktas: the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; the first Lokpal was appointed in March 2019.

These tools show that grassroots democracy is both a structure (panchayats) and a practice (asking questions).

cards.h: Strengths and limits of movement politics
cards.b:
Strengths: they widen participation, bring marginal issues to agenda, and often produce laws.

Limits and criticisms:

  • Fragmentation: many local struggles with no common platform.
  • Co-optation and NGO-isation: donor money can turn movements into project-driven bodies. The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 (amended in 2020) tightens foreign funds, and critics say it is also used to pressure dissenting groups.
  • Elite leadership: leaders are often middle class and urban; the poor may be followers.
  • State response: police action, cases under the UAPA or preventive laws, internet shutdowns, and bans on assembly.
  • Institutional gains can be undone: the RTI Act was amended in 2019 (tenure and pay of Information Commissioners) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 changed the personal-information exemption in section 8(1)(j); activists say this weakens transparency.
  • Exclusive demands: some movements (nativist, caste or communal) can threaten others' rights.

cards.h: Movements to cite from recent years
cards.b:
• Farmers 2020-21: repeal of the three farm laws (November 2021) and the demand for legal MSP (Delhi Chalo, 2024).
  • Anti-CAA protests (2019-20) including Shaheen Bagh, which led to a Supreme Court ruling that public roads cannot be blocked indefinitely.
  • Ladakh: demands for statehood and Sixth Schedule protection, with protests in September 2025 that turned violent in Leh. Activist Sonam Wangchuk was reported detained under the National Security Act.
  • Hasdeo Aranya (Chhattisgarh) against coal mining on forest land, and Great Nicobar project concerns.
  • Labour codes (November 2025): trade union protests.
  • RTI: a rise in pending appeals in Information Commissions and vacancies are repeated complaints.
  • Digital activism and citizen journalism extend the older repertoire.

Structure: define and place movements within civil society; theory (Kothari, Chatterjee, Omvedt); Gandhian and JP legacy; movements that produced laws (RTI, MGNREGA, FRA, Lokpal); livelihood and people's planning (SEWA, Kerala); critique (NGO-isation, state response, rollback); recent examples; conclude that movements and institutions need each other.
